lessons.title: Forces, Gravity and Resultant Forces
lessons.description: Scalar vs vector quantities, contact and non-contact forces, gravity, weight, and resultant forces.
lessons.content_html:
Scalars and Vectors

In physics, every quantity you measure falls into one of two categories. A scalar quantity has magnitude (size) only. A vector quantity has both magnitude and direction. Getting this distinction right is essential for the exam — questions often ask you to classify quantities correctly.

Scalar examples: mass (measured in kg), temperature (°C), time (s), speed (m/s), distance (m), and energy (J). Notice that speed tells you how fast something is going but not which way. Vector examples: force (N), velocity (m/s in a stated direction), displacement (m in a stated direction), and acceleration (m/s² in a stated direction). Velocity is the vector version of speed — it includes direction.

Key Fact

Scalar = magnitude only. Vector = magnitude + direction. A common exam mistake is confusing speed (scalar) with velocity (vector), or distance (scalar) with displacement (vector). Always check whether the question asks for a scalar or vector answer.

What Is a Force?

A force is a push or a pull that acts on an object. Forces are measured in newtons (N) using a Newton meter. Because forces have both magnitude and direction, they are vector quantities. Force arrows are used in diagrams to show the size and direction of a force — the longer the arrow, the bigger the force, and the arrow points in the direction the force acts.

Forces can change an object’s speed, direction of travel, or shape. A force does not always cause movement — it can also keep an object stationary by balancing another force. For GCSE, you need to understand two main categories of force: contact forces and non-contact forces.

Contact and Non-Contact Forces

A contact force acts when two objects are physically touching. Examples include friction (which opposes sliding motion between surfaces), air resistance (which slows objects moving through air), tension (the pulling force in a stretched rope or cable), the normal contact force (the support force a surface pushes back with), and upthrust (the upward force from a fluid on a submerged or floating object).

Friction: When you push a box across the floor, friction between the box and the floor opposes the movement. Friction generates thermal energy — rub your hands together and they warm up. Air resistance: A skydiver falling through the air experiences air resistance pushing upwards against their motion. Normal contact force: A book resting on a table is pushed upward by the table — this support force acts at right angles to the surface. Tension: When you pull a dog on a lead, the lead is under tension. Upthrust: A boat floats because the upthrust from the water equals its weight.

A non-contact force acts at a distance — the objects do not need to be touching. The three non-contact forces you need to know are gravitational force (the attraction between any two masses), electrostatic force (the attraction or repulsion between electric charges), and magnetic force (the attraction or repulsion between magnets or magnetic materials).

Key Fact

Contact forces require objects to touch: friction, air resistance, tension, normal contact force, upthrust. Non-contact forces act at a distance: gravitational, electrostatic, magnetic. The exam may give you a scenario and ask you to identify which type of force is acting.

Gravity and Gravitational Fields

Gravity is a non-contact force of attraction between any two objects that have mass. The more mass an object has, the stronger its gravitational pull. The Earth has a large mass, so it exerts a significant gravitational force on everything near it — this is what keeps us on the ground, pulls objects downward when dropped, and holds the Moon in orbit.

A gravitational field is the region around a mass where another mass would experience a gravitational force. The strength of this field is measured by the gravitational field strength (symbol: g), measured in newtons per kilogram (N/kg). On the surface of the Earth, g is approximately 9.8 N/kg. This means every kilogram of mass experiences a gravitational force of 9.8 N pulling it downward.

Gravitational field strength varies depending on the mass of the object creating the field and the distance from it. On the Moon, g is only about 1.6 N/kg (roughly one-sixth of Earth’s value), so objects weigh much less on the Moon even though their mass stays the same.

Weight, Mass, and the Equation

Mass is the amount of matter in an object. It is measured in kilograms (kg) and does not change wherever you go — your mass on Earth is the same as your mass on the Moon or in deep space.

Weight is the force acting on an object due to gravity. It is measured in newtons (N) and depends on where you are. Weight is calculated using the equation:

\(Weight = mass \times \text{gravitational field strength}\)

\(W = m \times g\)

where W is weight in newtons (N), m is mass in kilograms (kg), and g is gravitational field strength in N/kg. For example, a person with a mass of 70 kg on Earth weighs: W = 70 × 9.8 = 686 N. The same person on the Moon would weigh: W = 70 × 1.6 = 112 N. Their mass stays at 70 kg in both cases.

Students often confuse mass and weight. Remember: mass is measured in kg and does not change with location. Weight is measured in N and changes depending on the gravitational field strength. In everyday language people say “I weigh 70 kg” — but in physics, 70 kg is your mass, not your weight. Your weight on Earth would be about 686 N. Weight is a force, so it is a vector (it acts downward). Mass is a scalar.

Key Fact

\(W = m \times g.\) Weight is measured in newtons (N), mass in kilograms (kg), and gravitational field strength in N/kg. On Earth, g ≈ 9.8 N/kg. Weight changes with location; mass does not. Weight acts downward toward the centre of the Earth and is measured using a calibrated spring balance (Newton meter).

Resultant Forces

Most objects have more than one force acting on them at the same time. The resultant force is a single force that has the same effect as all the individual forces acting on an object combined. To find the resultant force when forces act along a straight line, add forces acting in the same direction and subtract forces acting in opposite directions.

Example 1: A car has an engine force of 3000 N driving it forward and air resistance of 1200 N acting backward. The resultant force = 3000 − 1200 = 1800 N forward. The car accelerates. Example 2: A book sits on a table. Its weight pushes down at 5 N and the normal contact force pushes up at 5 N. The resultant force = 5 − 5 = 0 N. The book is stationary (or moving at constant speed).

Resultant force = 0 (balanced forces): The object is either stationary or moving at a constant speed in a straight line. It does NOT necessarily mean the object is still — an aircraft flying at constant speed has balanced forces (thrust equals drag, lift equals weight). Resultant force ≠ 0 (unbalanced forces): The object accelerates in the direction of the resultant force. It could speed up, slow down, or change direction. Key point: A moving object does not need a force to keep moving at constant speed — it only needs a force to change its speed or direction.

Free Body Diagrams

A free body diagram is a simple sketch showing all the forces acting on a single object. Each force is drawn as a labelled arrow pointing in the direction it acts. The length of the arrow represents the relative size of the force — a bigger force gets a longer arrow.

To draw a free body diagram: (1) identify the object you are analysing, (2) draw it as a simple shape (usually a box or dot), (3) identify every force acting on the object, (4) draw each force as a labelled arrow from the object, pointing in the correct direction, (5) make the arrow lengths proportional to the force sizes. Free body diagrams help you work out the resultant force and predict how the object will move.

A skydiver who has just jumped from a plane has two forces acting on them: weight (gravitational force pulling downward, e.g. 800 N) and air resistance (pushing upward, e.g. 200 N at first). The weight arrow is drawn longer because it is the larger force. Resultant force = 800 − 200 = 600 N downward, so the skydiver accelerates downward. As they fall faster, air resistance increases until it equals weight — the resultant force becomes zero and the skydiver reaches terminal velocity (constant speed).
lessons.exam_tip_html: When the exam asks you to calculate weight, always write out W = m × g, substitute the values, then calculate the answer with the correct unit (N). For “describe” questions about forces, always state the type of force, its direction, and whether it is contact or non-contact. In resultant force questions, show your working clearly — state which forces act in which direction before adding or subtracting. A common 1-mark question is “What is meant by the term resultant force?” — the answer is: a single force that has the same effect as all the forces combined.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Scalars have magnitude only (speed, mass, distance); vectors have magnitude and direction (force, velocity, displacement). Force is always a vector.
  • Contact forces need objects to touch (friction, air resistance, tension, normal contact force, upthrust); non-contact forces act at a distance (gravity, electrostatic, magnetic).
  • Weight = mass × gravitational field strength (W = m × g). Mass is in kg and doesn’t change; weight is in N and depends on g. On Earth, g ≈ 9.8 N/kg.

1 mark(s) for the difference:

1 mark(s) for valid examples:
• Contact: friction / air resistance / tension / normal contact force / upthrust (1)
• Non-contact: gravity / gravitational force / electrostatic force / magnetic force (1)

practice_questions.text: An astronaut has a mass of 80 kg. The gravitational field strength on Mars is 3.7 N/kg. Calculate the weight of the astronaut on Mars. Give the unit.
practice_questions.marks:
Award marks as follows:
• Correct substitution: W = 80 × 3.7 (1)
• Correct answer: 296 N (1)

Allow ecf if substitution is shown but arithmetic is wrong (1 mark).
Unit mark included in the answer — must state N (newtons).

practice_questions.text: Explain why an object’s weight changes when it is taken from Earth to the Moon, but its mass stays the same.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 3 marks:
• Weight depends on gravitational field strength (g) (1)
• The Moon has a lower gravitational field strength than Earth / g on the Moon is about 1.6 N/kg compared to 9.8 N/kg on Earth (1)
• Mass is the amount of matter in an object and does not depend on location / gravitational field strength (1)

Accept: weight is a force caused by gravity so it changes; mass is a property of the object so it stays the same.

practice_questions.text: A car has a driving force of 4500 N from its engine. The total resistive force (friction and air resistance) acting on the car is 2800 N. Compare the forces acting on the car and explain what happens to its motion.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks:
• The driving force (4500 N) is greater than the resistive force (2800 N) (1)
• The resultant force is 4500 – 2800 = 1700 N (1)
• The resultant force acts in the direction of the driving force / forward (1)
• The car accelerates / speeds up (in the forward direction) because there is an unbalanced resultant force (1)

Accept references to Newton’s first law (an object changes speed when a resultant force acts on it).

practice_questions.text: A student says: ‘If the resultant force on an object is zero, the object must be stationary.’ Explain why the student is not correct. Use the idea of balanced forces in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Indicative content:
• A resultant force of zero means the forces are balanced
• Balanced forces mean no change in motion / no acceleration
• The object could be stationary OR moving at a constant speed in a straight line
• Example: an aircraft flying at constant speed has thrust equal to drag and lift equal to weight — resultant force is zero but the aircraft is moving
• A force is only needed to change speed or direction, not to maintain constant speed
• Reference to Newton’s first law: an object remains at rest or continues at constant velocity unless acted on by a resultant force
Top band (5-6): Clear and detailed explanation with correct use of terminology, at least one relevant example, and explicit reference to balanced forces not meaning stationary.
Mid band (3-4): Correct explanation that the object could be moving at constant speed but limited development or example.
Lower band (1-2): Basic statement that the object could be moving, with limited or no explanation of why.

lessons.title: Work Done, Elasticity and Hooke's Law
lessons.description: How forces do work to transfer energy, elastic and inelastic deformation, and the spring constant.
lessons.content_html:
Work Done

When a force causes an object to move through a distance, work is done on the object. Work done is simply another way of saying energy has been transferred. The force must act in the direction of movement (or have a component in that direction) for work to be done.

Key Fact

Work done (J) = force (N) × distance (m), or W = Fs. One joule of work is done when a force of one newton moves an object through a distance of one metre.

For example, if a person pushes a box with a force of 50 N over a distance of 3 m, the work done is 50 × 3 = 150 J. This 150 J of energy has been transferred from the person’s chemical energy store to the kinetic energy store of the box (and some to thermal energy through friction).

Work done against friction causes a rise in the temperature of the object and its surroundings. This is because kinetic energy is being transferred to the thermal energy stores of the surfaces in contact. You can feel this by rubbing your hands together quickly — the friction between your palms transfers energy to heat.

A cyclist applies a force of 200 N to pedal along a flat road for 1500 m. Calculate the work done by the cyclist.

Step 1: Write the equation: W = Fs
Step 2: Substitute the values: W = 200 × 1500
Step 3: Calculate: W = 300,000 J (or 300 kJ)

The cyclist has transferred 300 kJ of energy. In practice, not all of this goes to the kinetic energy store — some is dissipated through friction and air resistance, raising the temperature of the surroundings.

Elastic and Inelastic Deformation

When a force is applied to an object and it changes shape, we say the object has been deformed. There are two types of deformation that you need to know:

Elastic deformation occurs when an object returns to its original shape and length after the force is removed. A stretched spring that bounces back to its normal length is an example of elastic deformation. The energy stored during elastic deformation is recoverable.

Inelastic deformation occurs when an object does not return to its original shape after the force is removed. It has been permanently deformed. A crushed drinks can is an example of inelastic deformation. The energy transferred during inelastic deformation is not fully recoverable — some is dissipated as heat.

Key Fact

Elastic deformation — the object returns to its original shape (energy is recoverable). Inelastic deformation — the object is permanently changed (energy is not fully recoverable). A spring can undergo either type depending on how far it is stretched.

Hooke’s Law and the Spring Constant

Hooke’s law states that the extension of an elastic object (such as a spring) is directly proportional to the force applied to it, as long as the limit of proportionality is not exceeded. This means that doubling the force doubles the extension.

The equation for Hooke’s law is:

Key Fact

Force (N) = spring constant (N/m) × extension (m), or F = ke. The spring constant (k) tells you how stiff the spring is — a higher spring constant means a stiffer spring that requires more force to extend it by a given amount.

For example, if a spring has a spring constant of 25 N/m and is extended by 0.2 m, the force required is F = 25 × 0.2 = 5 N. The spring constant is measured in newtons per metre (N/m) and the extension must be measured in metres for the equation to work correctly.

In this practical, you investigate the relationship between force and extension for a spring. Set up a clamp stand with a spring hanging from a clamp, and a ruler positioned vertically beside it. Measure the natural (unloaded) length of the spring. Then add known weights (e.g. 1 N at a time) and measure the new length each time. The extension equals the new length minus the original length.

Plot a graph of force (y-axis) against extension (x-axis). The graph should show a straight line through the origin up to the limit of proportionality, confirming Hooke’s law. The gradient of the straight-line section gives the spring constant (k). Beyond the limit of proportionality, the line curves — the spring no longer obeys Hooke’s law and may be permanently deformed.

Force–Extension Graphs

A force–extension graph for a spring that obeys Hooke’s law shows a straight line through the origin. The gradient of this straight line is equal to the spring constant (k). Beyond the limit of proportionality, the graph bends towards the extension axis — the spring extends more for each additional unit of force, and it will not return to its original length when the force is removed.

The elastic limit is closely related to the limit of proportionality. Beyond the elastic limit, the spring undergoes inelastic (permanent) deformation. In many exam questions, the limit of proportionality and elastic limit are treated as essentially the same point on the graph.

When you see a force–extension graph in the exam: the straight-line section shows the region where Hooke’s law applies (force is proportional to extension). The point where the line begins to curve is the limit of proportionality. If asked to find the spring constant from a graph, pick any point on the straight section and divide force by extension: k = F ÷ e. Remember that the area under a force–extension graph represents the energy stored in the spring (elastic potential energy).

Elastic Potential Energy

When a spring is stretched or compressed within its limit of proportionality, energy is stored in its elastic potential energy store. This energy can be recovered when the spring is released — for example, a catapult transfers elastic potential energy into kinetic energy when it fires a stone.

Key Fact

Elastic potential energy (J) = ½ × spring constant (N/m) × extension² (m²), or \(E_{e} = \frac{1}{2}ke^{2}\). This equation is given on the equation sheet in the exam, but you must be able to use and rearrange it.

For example, a spring with k = 25 N/m extended by 0.2 m stores: Ee = ½ × 25 × 0.2² = ½ × 25 × 0.04 = 0.5 J. Notice that because extension is squared, doubling the extension quadruples the energy stored. This equation only applies when the spring has not been stretched beyond its limit of proportionality.
lessons.exam_tip_html: In “calculate” questions, always write the equation first, then substitute values, then calculate — you earn marks for each step even if your final answer is wrong. Watch the units: extension must be in metres (not cm) when using F = ke or Ee = ½ke². For “explain” questions about elastic vs inelastic deformation, make sure you state what happens to the shape AND what happens to the energy. In graph questions, practise identifying the limit of proportionality and calculating the spring constant from the gradient.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Work done (W = Fs) measures the energy transferred when a force moves an object. Work done against friction causes a temperature rise.
  • Elastic deformation means the object returns to its original shape; inelastic deformation means it is permanently changed. Hooke’s law (F = ke) applies up to the limit of proportionality.
  • Elastic potential energy (Ee = ½ke²) is stored in a stretched or compressed spring. The energy stored is proportional to the square of the extension.

practice_questions.text: A student investigated the relationship between force and extension for a spring. The results showed a straight line through the origin up to 6 N, then the line curved. Compare the behaviour of the spring below 6 N and above 6 N, and explain the significance of the point where the line begins to curve.

• Below 6 N the force is directly proportional to the extension / the spring obeys Hooke’s law (1).
• Above 6 N the spring no longer obeys Hooke’s law / the extension is no longer proportional to the force (1).
• The point where the line begins to curve is the limit of proportionality (1).
• Beyond this point the spring may be permanently / inelastically deformed and will not return to its original length (1).

practice_questions.text: A student stretches a spring and measures the extension for different forces. The spring has a spring constant of 50 N/m. Describe how the student should carry out this investigation, including the equipment needed and how to ensure accurate results. Calculate the extension when a force of 3 N is applied.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (5-6): A detailed and coherent account of the practical method, including equipment (clamp stand, spring, ruler, masses/newton meter), method (measure natural length, add weights, measure new length, calculate extension), accuracy measures (repeat readings, eye level reading, ensure spring hangs freely), and a correct calculation of extension.
Mid band (3-4): Describes the method with some detail but may lack accuracy improvements or the calculation may contain an error.
Lower band (1-2): Simple statements about the method or calculation with limited detail.
Indicative content:
• Equipment: clamp stand, boss, clamp, spring, ruler, known masses or newton meter, set square.
• Measure the natural (unloaded) length of the spring using the ruler.
• Add known weights one at a time and measure the new length.
• Extension = new length – original length.
• Repeat each measurement and calculate a mean to improve accuracy.
• Read the ruler at eye level to avoid parallax error.
• Calculation: F = ke, so e = F/k = 3/50 = 0.06 m (or 6 cm).

lessons.title: Speed, Velocity and Acceleration
lessons.description: Calculating speed, velocity and acceleration using equations and motion graphs.
lessons.content_html:
Distance and Displacement

Before you can understand motion properly, you need to know the difference between distance and displacement. Distance is the total length of the path an object travels — it doesn’t matter which direction. If you walk 3 m north and then 3 m south, you’ve covered a distance of 6 m. Displacement, however, measures the straight-line distance from start to finish in a given direction. In the same example, your displacement is 0 m because you ended up back where you started.

Key Fact

Distance is a scalar quantity (magnitude only). Displacement is a vector quantity (magnitude and direction). The specification requires you to know this distinction.

This difference between scalar and vector quantities runs through the whole of this topic. Scalars have size only; vectors have both size and direction. You will meet this again with speed and velocity.

Speed and Velocity

The quantity known as speed tells you how fast an object is moving. It is calculated using the equation:

Key Fact

\(speed = distance \div time\)   or   \(v = s \div t\)
where v = speed in m/s, s = distance in m, t = time in s.

Speed is a scalar — it has no direction. velocity on the other hand, is the speed in a stated direction, making it a vector. An object moving at 5 m/s to the east has a velocity of 5 m/s east. If it turns around and moves at the same speed to the west, its speed is still 5 m/s but its velocity has changed to 5 m/s west.

the specification expects you to recall typical speeds for everyday situations:

  • Walking: approximately 1.5 m/s
  • Running: approximately 3 m/s
  • Cycling: approximately 6 m/s
  • Car on a road: approximately 13–30 m/s
  • Train: approximately 50 m/s
  • Aeroplane: approximately 250 m/s
  • Sound in air: approximately 330 m/s

These values are approximate. Speed varies with age, terrain, fitness, weather, and other factors. In the exam, you may be asked to estimate a speed or explain why it changes.

Distance–Time Graphs

A distance–time graph plots distance on the y-axis against time on the x-axis. The key rule is simple: the gradient of the line equals the speed.

Key Fact

On a distance–time graph: a horizontal line means the object is stationary, a straight diagonal line means constant speed, and a curve means the speed is changing (accelerating or decelerating).

To find the speed at any point on a curve, draw a tangent to the curve at that point and calculate its gradient. The gradient is calculated as the change in distance divided by the change in time (rise ÷ run).

Velocity–Time Graphs

A velocity–time graph plots velocity on the y-axis against time on the x-axis. These graphs tell you two things:

  • The gradient of the line gives the acceleration of the object.
  • The area under the line gives the distance travelled (or displacement).

A horizontal line on a velocity–time graph means constant velocity (zero acceleration). A line sloping upwards means the object is accelerating. A line sloping downwards means deceleration (negative acceleration). To calculate the area under a straight-line graph, split it into rectangles and triangles and add the areas together.

A car accelerates from rest to 20 m/s in 10 seconds, then travels at a constant 20 m/s for 5 seconds.

Acceleration phase: gradient = (20 − 0) ÷ (10 − 0) = 2 m/s². The area under this section is a triangle: ½ × 10 × 20 = 100 m.

Constant speed phase: gradient = 0 (no acceleration). The area under this section is a rectangle: 5 × 20 = 100 m.

Total distance: 100 + 100 = 200 m.

Acceleration

The quantity acceleration is the rate at which velocity changes. It is calculated using:

Key Fact

\(acceleration = \text{change in velocity} \div \text{time taken}\)   or   \(a = (v - u) \div t\)
where a = acceleration in m/s², v = final velocity in m/s, u = initial velocity in m/s, t = time in s.

A positive value for acceleration means the object is speeding up. A negative value means it is slowing down (decelerating). Near the surface of the Earth, an object in free fall accelerates at approximately 9.8 m/s² due to gravity (often rounded to 10 m/s² in calculations).

For objects undergoing uniform acceleration (constant acceleration), you need to use this equation:

\(v^{2} = u^{2} + 2as\)
where v = final velocity (m/s), u = initial velocity (m/s), a = acceleration (m/s²), s = distance (m).

This equation is particularly useful when you are not given a time value. For example, a cyclist accelerates uniformly from 4 m/s at 0.5 m/s² over a distance of 50 m. To find the final velocity: v² = 4² + 2 × 0.5 × 50 = 16 + 50 = 66. So v = √66 ≈ 8.1 m/s.

A car increases its velocity from 10 m/s to 25 m/s in 5 seconds. Calculate its acceleration.

Step 1: Write the equation: a = (v − u) ÷ t
Step 2: Substitute: a = (25 − 10) ÷ 5
Step 3: Calculate: a = 15 ÷ 5 = \(3\,m/s^{2}\)
lessons.exam_tip_html: In calculation questions, always write the equation first, then substitute your values, then calculate. You earn marks for each step even if you get the final answer wrong. For graph questions, draw clear construction lines when finding gradients or areas — the examiner needs to see how you read values from the graph. Remember: gradient of a distance–time graph = speed, gradient of a velocity–time graph = acceleration, area under a velocity–time graph = distance.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Distance is scalar (no direction); displacement is vector (has direction). Speed is scalar; velocity is vector. Use v = s ÷ t for speed and a = (v − u) ÷ t for acceleration.
  • On a distance–time graph, the gradient gives speed. On a velocity–time graph, the gradient gives acceleration and the area under the line gives distance travelled.
  • For uniform acceleration without a time value, use v² = u² + 2as. Always show your working in calculation questions for full marks.

lessons.title: Newton's Laws of Motion
lessons.description: Newton's three laws of motion, inertia, F=ma calculations, and action-reaction pairs.
lessons.content_html:
Newton’s First Law — The Law of Inertia

An object at rest will stay at rest, and an object in motion will continue moving at a constant velocity, unless acted upon by a resultant force. This is Newton’s first law of motion. It tells us that forces are not needed to keep something moving — they are only needed to change the way it moves.

If the resultant force on an object is zero, the object is in equilibrium. A book resting on a table has weight pulling it down and a normal contact force pushing it up. These two forces are equal and opposite, so the resultant force is zero and the book stays still.

Key Fact

Newton’s first law: If the resultant force on an object is zero, it remains stationary or continues to move at a constant velocity in a straight line. No resultant force means no change in motion.

A moving object also obeys this law. A spacecraft in deep space, far from any gravitational pull, will keep travelling at the same speed in the same direction forever because there is no resultant force to slow it down or change its direction. On Earth, friction and air resistance act as forces that slow things down, which is why objects eventually stop — not because they “run out” of motion.

inertia is the tendency of an object to resist any change in its motion. The more massive an object is, the greater its inertia. A heavy shopping trolley is harder to start moving and harder to stop than an empty one — it has more inertia because it has more mass.

inertial mass is defined as the ratio of force to acceleration. It can be found using the equation m = F ÷ a. A larger inertial mass means a greater force is needed to produce the same acceleration. This is a Higher Tier concept that links Newton’s first and second laws together.

Newton’s Second Law — Force, Mass and Acceleration

Newton’s second law states that the acceleration of an object is directly proportional to the resultant force acting on it, and inversely proportional to its mass. The equation is:

Key Fact

F = m × a — Resultant force (N) = mass (kg) × acceleration (m/s²). You must be able to recall this equation and rearrange it confidently.

This law explains why a greater force causes a greater acceleration, and why a heavier object accelerates less for the same force. If you push an empty shopping trolley and a full one with the same force, the empty trolley accelerates more because it has less mass.

To rearrange the equation: a = F ÷ m (to find acceleration) or m = F ÷ a (to find mass). Always check your units — force in newtons (N), mass in kilograms (kg), and acceleration in metres per second squared (m/s²).

Question: A car has a mass of 1,200 kg and accelerates at 2.5 m/s². Calculate the resultant force acting on the car.

Answer: F = m × a = 1,200 × 2.5 = 3,000 N. The resultant force is 3,000 N (or 3 kN).

Question: A resultant force of 4,500 N acts on a van of mass 1,500 kg. What is its acceleration?

Answer: a = F ÷ m = 4,500 ÷ 1,500 = 3 m/s².

Weight, Mass and Gravitational Field Strength

Weight is the force acting on an object due to gravity. It is calculated using W = m × g, where W is weight in newtons (N), m is mass in kilograms (kg), and g is the gravitational field strength in N/kg. On Earth, g = 9.8 N/kg.

Mass is a scalar quantity — it stays the same wherever you are. Weight is a vector quantity — it changes depending on the gravitational field strength. An astronaut on the Moon has the same mass as on Earth, but their weight is about one-sixth because the Moon’s gravitational field strength is lower.

Terminal Velocity

When an object falls through a fluid (such as air or water), it initially accelerates because the force of gravity (weight) is greater than the drag force. As the object speeds up, the drag force increases.

Eventually, the drag force becomes equal to the weight. The resultant force is now zero, so the object stops accelerating and falls at a constant speed. This maximum constant speed is called terminal velocity.

Key Fact

At terminal velocity, the resultant force on the object is zero. Weight acts downwards and drag acts upwards — they are balanced. The object has zero acceleration but is still moving.

A skydiver initially accelerates at about 9.8 m/s² (free fall). As their speed increases, air resistance builds. Terminal velocity is reached after about 10–15 seconds of freefall. When they open a parachute, the surface area increases dramatically, drag force exceeds weight, and they decelerate until a new, much lower terminal velocity is reached — slow enough to land safely.

Newton’s Third Law — Action and Reaction

Newton’s third law states: whenever two objects interact, they exert equal and opposite forces on each other. These are called action-reaction pairs.

When you push against a wall, the wall pushes back on you with the same force. When a swimmer pushes water backwards with their hands, the water pushes the swimmer forwards. The two forces in a pair always act on different objects, are the same type of force, and are equal in magnitude but opposite in direction.

Students often confuse Newton’s third law pairs with balanced forces. A book on a table has weight acting downwards and a normal contact force acting upwards — these are not a third law pair because they both act on the same object (the book). A true third law pair involves two different objects: the book pulls the Earth towards it (gravitational attraction), and the Earth pulls the book downward (weight). These act on different objects and are the same type of force (gravitational).

Key test for a third law pair: the two forces must be the same type, equal in size, opposite in direction, and act on two different objects.

Walking: Your foot pushes backwards on the ground (friction), and the ground pushes your foot forwards — this is what propels you forward.

Rocket launch: The rocket pushes exhaust gases downwards, and the exhaust gases push the rocket upwards. The forces are equal and opposite, acting on different objects (rocket and gas).

Sitting on a chair: You push down on the chair with a contact force, and the chair pushes up on you with an equal contact force. Meanwhile, the chair pushes down on the floor, and the floor pushes up on the chair — a separate pair.
lessons.exam_tip_html: In calculation questions using F = m × a, always show your working clearly: write the equation, substitute the values with units, then calculate. If the question asks you to “explain” Newton’s third law, make sure you identify both objects, state the forces are equal in size and opposite in direction, and emphasise they act on different objects. A common mistake is describing balanced forces on one object instead of an action-reaction pair on two objects.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Newton’s first law: an object remains at rest or at constant velocity unless acted on by a resultant force. Inertia is an object’s resistance to change in motion and depends on mass.
  • Newton’s second law: F = m × a. Greater force means greater acceleration; greater mass means less acceleration for the same force. At terminal velocity, the resultant force is zero.
  • Newton’s third law: every action has an equal and opposite reaction. The two forces in a pair always act on different objects and are the same type of force.

lessons.title: Stopping Distances, Braking and Momentum
lessons.description: Thinking and braking distance, factors affecting stopping, and conservation of momentum.
lessons.content_html:
Stopping Distance

Every time a driver spots a hazard and brings a vehicle to a halt, the car travels a certain distance before it stops completely. This total distance is called the stopping distance. It is made up of two parts: the thinking distance and the braking distance.

Key Fact

Stopping distance = thinking distance + braking distance. You must learn this equation — it is tested often.

Thinking Distance

Thinking distance is the distance the car travels during the driver’s reaction time — the time between seeing the hazard and pressing the brake pedal. A typical human reaction time is between 0.2 and 0.9 seconds.

Several factors can increase thinking distance by increasing reaction time:

Tiredness — a tired driver reacts more slowly because the nervous system processes signals less efficiently.

Alcohol and drugs — these substances slow down the transmission of nerve impulses, increasing reaction time significantly.

Distractions — using a mobile phone or adjusting the radio diverts attention, delaying the moment the driver notices a hazard.

Speed — thinking distance is directly proportional to speed. At higher speeds, the car covers more ground during the same reaction time.

Braking Distance

Braking distance is the distance the vehicle travels after the brakes are applied until it comes to rest. When the brakes are pressed, a braking force acts on the wheels, doing work to transfer kinetic energy into heat energy in the brakes.

Wet or icy roads — reduced friction between the tyres and the road surface means less braking force can be applied.

Worn tyres or brakes — worn tread on tyres reduces grip. Worn brake pads reduce the braking force.

Higher speed — a faster vehicle has more kinetic energy, so more work must be done by the braking force to bring it to rest.

Greater mass — a heavier vehicle has more kinetic energy at the same speed, so the braking distance increases.

Key Fact

When a vehicle brakes, the brakes do work to transfer kinetic energy to thermal energy in the brakes. In an emergency stop at high speed, a very large braking force can cause the brakes to overheat and the vehicle to skid.

Measuring Reaction Time

Reaction time can be measured using a simple ruler-drop experiment. One person holds a ruler vertically and drops it without warning, while the other person catches it as quickly as possible. The distance the ruler falls before being caught is used to calculate the reaction time using the equation for acceleration due to gravity.

In the exam, you may be asked to describe this experiment and explain how to improve accuracy — for example, by repeating the test and calculating a mean, or by making sure the catcher’s hand is level with the zero mark at the start.

Momentum

Momentum is a property of every moving object. It depends on both the mass and the velocity of the object. The equation is:

Key Fact

p = m × v — where p is momentum (kg m/s), m is mass (kg), and v is velocity (m/s). Momentum is a vector quantity, so its direction matters.

For example, a car of mass 1200 kg travelling at 15 m/s has a momentum of 1200 × 15 = 18,000 kg m/s. If the same car were stationary, its momentum would be zero because its velocity is zero.

Conservation of Momentum

In a closed system, the total momentum before an event is always equal to the total momentum after the event. This is called the conservation of momentum.

A 2 kg trolley moving at 3 m/s collides with a stationary 1 kg trolley. After the collision they stick together and move as one object. What is their velocity after the collision?

Step 1: Total momentum before = (2 × 3) + (1 × 0) = 6 kg m/s.

Step 2: Total momentum after = total mass × velocity = (2 + 1) × v = 3v.

Step 3: By conservation of momentum, 3v = 6, so v = 2 m/s.

Conservation of momentum applies to all collisions and explosions in a closed system. In an explosion, the total momentum before is zero (the objects are stationary), so the total momentum after must also be zero — the objects move apart with equal and opposite momenta.

When a force acts on an object, it causes a change in momentum. The relationship is: force = change in momentum ÷ time taken, or F = Δp ÷ Δt. A larger braking force produces a greater rate of change of momentum, bringing the vehicle to a stop in a shorter time (and shorter distance).

This also explains why safety features such as crumple zones and airbags work. They increase the time over which the change in momentum happens, which reduces the force on the occupants and lowers the risk of injury.

Key Fact

Safety features like crumple zones, seat belts, and airbags increase the time over which momentum changes during a collision. By increasing the time, the force on passengers is reduced (F = Δp ÷ Δt).
lessons.exam_tip_html: Stopping distance questions often ask you to explain factors — always link each factor back to either thinking distance or braking distance, never just “stopping distance” on its own. For momentum calculations, show every step clearly: write the equation, substitute values, and give the unit (kg m/s). If asked to “explain” conservation of momentum, state that total momentum before equals total momentum after in a closed system, then prove it with numbers.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Stopping distance = thinking distance + braking distance. Thinking distance depends on reaction time and speed; braking distance depends on speed, road conditions, tyre condition, and vehicle mass.
  • Momentum (p = mv) is a vector quantity measured in kg m/s. In a closed system, total momentum is always conserved.
  • Safety features work by increasing the time over which momentum changes, reducing the force on passengers (F = Δp ÷ Δt).

lessons.title: Waves: Properties and Behaviour
lessons.description: Transverse and longitudinal waves, wave properties, the wave equation v = fλ, and ripple tanks.
lessons.content_html:
What Are Waves?

A wave is a disturbance that transfers energy from one place to another without transferring matter. When you drop a stone into a pond, ripples spread outward — the water itself does not travel across the pond, but the energy does. This is the key idea behind all waves: energy is transferred, but the particles of the medium return to their original position after the wave passes.

Waves can travel through a medium (such as water, air, or a solid) or, in the case of electromagnetic waves, through a vacuum. In this lesson we focus on mechanical waves — waves that require a medium to travel through.

Key Fact

Waves transfer energy without transferring matter. The particles of the medium oscillate (vibrate) about a fixed point but do not travel with the wave.

Transverse Waves

In a transverse wave, the oscillations of the particles are perpendicular (at right angles) to the direction in which the wave travels. Think of a rope: if you flick one end up and down, the wave moves horizontally along the rope, but each point on the rope moves up and down.

The highest point of a transverse wave is called the crest (or peak), and the lowest point is called the trough. Examples of transverse waves include water surface waves, light waves, and all other electromagnetic waves. S-waves produced by earthquakes are also transverse.

Longitudinal Waves

In a longitudinal wave, the oscillations of the particles are parallel to the direction in which the wave travels. A slinky spring demonstrates this well: if you push and pull one end back and forth, regions where the coils bunch together (compressions) and regions where they spread apart (rarefactions) move along the spring.

Sound is the most common example of a longitudinal wave. When a speaker vibrates, it pushes air molecules together and pulls them apart, creating compressions and rarefactions that travel through the air to your ear. P-waves from earthquakes are also longitudinal.

Key Fact

Transverse: oscillations perpendicular to direction of travel (e.g. light, water surface waves). Longitudinal: oscillations parallel to direction of travel (e.g. sound). Both types transfer energy, not matter.

Transverse waves have crests and troughs. The particles move up and down (or side to side) while the wave moves forward. Examples: light, radio waves, water surface ripples, S-waves.

Longitudinal waves have compressions and rarefactions. The particles move back and forth in the same direction as the wave. Examples: sound waves, ultrasound, P-waves.

A useful way to remember: “Transverse = T = The oscillations go 'T'all (up and down)”. In longitudinal waves, the particles move “along” the direction of travel.

Wave Properties

All waves — whether transverse or longitudinal — can be described using four key properties:

Amplitude — the amplitude is the maximum displacement of a point on the wave from its undisturbed (rest) position. For a transverse wave, it is the distance from the rest position to the top of a crest (or bottom of a trough). A larger amplitude means the wave carries more energy. Amplitude is measured in metres (m).

Wavelength — the wavelength (λ, the Greek letter lambda) is the distance from one point on a wave to the equivalent point on the next wave — for example, from crest to crest or trough to trough. Wavelength is measured in metres (m).

Frequency — the frequency (f) is the number of complete waves that pass a fixed point each second. It is measured in hertz (Hz). A frequency of 100 Hz means 100 complete waves pass every second.

Period — the period (T) is the time taken for one complete wave to pass a point. It is the inverse of frequency: T = 1 ÷ f. If a wave has a frequency of 50 Hz, its period is 1 ÷ 50 = 0.02 seconds.

Wave Speed and the Wave Equation

Wave speed (v) is the speed at which the wave front moves through the medium. It is measured in metres per second (m/s). Wave speed, frequency, and wavelength are linked by a simple equation that you must learn for the exam:

Key Fact

Wave equation: wave speed = frequency × wavelength, or \(v = f \times \lambda\). Units: v in m/s, f in Hz, λ in m. You must be able to rearrange this to find any of the three quantities.

To rearrange: \(f = v \div \lambda\) and \(\lambda = v \div f\). Always check your units before substituting — convert centimetres to metres (divide by 100) and kilometres to metres (multiply by 1000).

Example 1: A water wave has a frequency of 4 Hz and a wavelength of 3 m. Calculate the wave speed.
v = f × λ = 4 × 3 = 12 m/s

Example 2: Microwaves have a wavelength of 12 cm and travel at 3 × 10⁸ m/s. Calculate the frequency.
First convert: 12 cm = 0.12 m.
f = v ÷ λ = (3 × 10⁸) ÷ 0.12 = \(2.5 \times 10^{9} Hz\)

Example 3: A sound wave has a frequency of 256 Hz and travels at 340 m/s. Calculate the wavelength.
λ = v ÷ f = 340 ÷ 256 = 1.33 m (to 3 s.f.)

Measuring Waves: The Ripple Tank

A ripple tank is a piece of apparatus used in required practical work to investigate the properties of waves in water. A motor-driven dipper creates regular waves on the surface of shallow water. A lamp above the tank projects the wave pattern onto a white card below, making the crests and troughs visible as bright and dark lines.

To measure the wavelength, you can use a ruler to measure the distance across several wave crests and then divide by the number of waves. For example, if 10 wavelengths span 30 cm, the wavelength is 30 ÷ 10 = 3 cm (0.03 m). Measuring multiple wavelengths and dividing gives a more accurate result than measuring a single wave.

To measure frequency, count the number of waves passing a fixed point in a known time using a stopwatch. For example, if 20 waves pass in 10 seconds, the frequency is 20 ÷ 10 = 2 Hz. Once you know the wavelength and frequency, you can calculate the wave speed using v = f × λ.

Method: Set up the ripple tank with a motor-driven dipper. Switch on the lamp above the tank. Adjust the frequency of the dipper and observe the wave pattern projected below. Use a ruler to measure the distance across several wavelengths and calculate the wavelength. Count waves passing a point over a set time to determine frequency. Calculate wave speed using v = f × λ.

Key tips: Use a stroboscope (flashing light) to “freeze” the wave pattern, making measurements easier. Measure across as many wavelengths as possible to reduce percentage error. Keep the water depth constant across the tank for consistent results. Note that changing the depth of water changes the wave speed.

Common Exam Pitfalls

Students often confuse amplitude with wavelength. Remember: amplitude is measured vertically (rest position to crest), while wavelength is measured horizontally (crest to crest). Another common error is forgetting to convert units — wavelengths given in cm or nm must be converted to metres before using the wave equation. Finally, remember that increasing the amplitude does not change the frequency or wavelength; it only changes the energy carried by the wave.
lessons.exam_tip_html: In “calculate” questions on waves, always write out the equation first (v = f × λ), show your substitution with correct units, then give the answer with the right unit. Examiners award marks for each step. When asked to “compare” transverse and longitudinal waves, structure your answer with one similarity and one difference — and always refer to the direction of oscillation relative to the direction of energy transfer.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Waves transfer energy without transferring matter. Transverse waves oscillate perpendicular to the direction of travel (e.g. light); longitudinal waves oscillate parallel (e.g. sound).
  • The four key wave properties are amplitude, wavelength, frequency, and period. Amplitude is vertical (rest to crest); wavelength is horizontal (crest to crest).
  • The wave equation v = f × λ links wave speed, frequency, and wavelength — learn it, practise rearranging it, and always convert units to SI before calculating.

lessons.title: The Electromagnetic Spectrum
lessons.description: The seven types of EM wave, their properties, everyday uses, and dangers across the spectrum.
lessons.content_html:
What Are Electromagnetic Waves?

Electromagnetic waves (EM waves) are transverse waves that transfer energy from one place to another. Unlike sound waves, they do not need a medium to travel through — they can pass through a vacuum (empty space). All electromagnetic waves travel at the same speed through a vacuum: 3 × 108 m/s, the speed of light.

EM waves are produced when charged particles oscillate (vibrate). They consist of oscillating electric and magnetic fields that are perpendicular to each other and to the direction the wave travels. The key equation linking wave speed, frequency, and wavelength is:

Key Fact

\(\text{wave speed} = frequency \times wavelength\)   (v = f × λ). For all EM waves in a vacuum, v = 3 × 108 m/s. This means waves with a higher frequency have a shorter wavelength, and waves with a lower frequency have a longer wavelength.

The Electromagnetic Spectrum

The electromagnetic spectrum is the entire range of EM waves, arranged in order of wavelength and frequency. There are seven main types, and you must learn them in order from longest wavelength to shortest:

\(Radio waves \rightarrow Microwaves \rightarrow Infrared \rightarrow Visible light \rightarrow Ultraviolet \rightarrow X-rays \rightarrow Gamma rays\)

As you move from radio waves to gamma rays, the frequency increases and the wavelength decreases. The boundaries between different types are not sharp — the spectrum is continuous, and one type blends gradually into the next.

A common mnemonic is: Running Men In Vests Usually X-ray Giraffes (Radio, Microwaves, Infrared, Visible, Ultraviolet, X-rays, Gamma). Alternatively, remember that the spectrum goes from the longest waves you encounter daily (radio) to the most energetic and penetrating (gamma). In the exam, being able to place any given wave type in the correct position on the spectrum is a frequently tested skill.

Radio Waves and Microwaves

Radio waves have the longest wavelength and lowest frequency of all EM waves. Wavelengths range from about 1 mm to several kilometres. They are used for television and radio broadcasts, Bluetooth, Wi-Fi, and communication with satellites. Radio waves can diffract (bend) around hills and buildings, which is why you can receive radio signals even when you are not in direct line of sight of the transmitter.

Microwaves have shorter wavelengths than radio waves (roughly 1 mm to 30 cm). They are used in satellite communications, mobile phone signals, and microwave ovens. In a microwave oven, the waves are absorbed by water molecules in food, causing them to vibrate and heat up. Microwaves can penetrate through the atmosphere and clouds, making them ideal for satellite transmissions.

Infrared Radiation

Infrared radiation (IR) is emitted by all objects that have a temperature above absolute zero. The hotter an object is, the more infrared it emits. This is the basis of thermal imaging cameras, which detect temperature differences and display them as colour maps — used by firefighters to find people in smoke-filled buildings, and by police helicopters to track suspects at night.

Other uses include electric heaters and toasters (which emit infrared to warm food and rooms), TV remote controls, optical fibre communication, and cooking. When infrared is absorbed by the skin, it is felt as warmth. Excessive exposure can cause skin burns.

Visible Light

Visible light is the only part of the EM spectrum that the human eye can detect. It occupies a very narrow band between infrared and ultraviolet. White light is made up of a continuous spectrum of colours — red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, and violet — which can be separated using a prism. Red light has the longest wavelength within this band, and violet has the shortest.

Visible light is used for vision (obviously), photography, fibre optic communication, and illumination. Different surfaces absorb, reflect, or transmit different wavelengths, which is why objects appear as different colours. A red shirt, for example, reflects red wavelengths and absorbs most other colours.

Ultraviolet Radiation

Ultraviolet radiation (UV) has a shorter wavelength and higher frequency than visible light. The Sun is the main natural source of UV. It is also produced by sun lamps and tanning beds. UV radiation causes the skin to produce vitamin D, which is essential for healthy bones.

However, overexposure to UV can cause sunburn, premature skin ageing, and increases the risk of skin cancer. UV can also damage the eyes, potentially leading to cataracts. Protective measures include wearing sunscreen, sunglasses, and limiting time in direct sunlight. UV is used to detect forged banknotes (special inks fluoresce under UV), in sterilisation of water and medical equipment, and in energy-efficient fluorescent lamps.

Key Fact

UV, X-rays, and gamma rays have enough energy to cause ionisation — they can knock electrons out of atoms, creating ions. This is why they are called ionising radiation. Ionising radiation can damage cells and DNA, increasing the risk of cancer.

X-rays

X-rays have very short wavelengths and very high frequencies. They can pass through soft body tissue but are absorbed by dense materials such as bone and metal. This property makes them invaluable in medicine for producing images of bones to check for fractures, and in airport security scanners to inspect luggage.

Medical X-rays work because bone absorbs X-rays more than soft tissue. A photographic plate or digital detector is placed behind the patient, and an X-ray beam is passed through the body. Bones appear white on the image (they block the X-rays), while soft tissue appears darker (X-rays pass through). CT scans use X-rays taken from multiple angles to build a detailed 3D image of internal organs and structures.

Because X-rays are ionising, radiographers take precautions: they stand behind lead-lined screens, patients wear lead aprons to protect areas not being imaged, and exposure times are kept as short as possible. The benefits of diagnosis must outweigh the small risk of cell damage from the radiation.

Gamma Rays

Gamma rays have the shortest wavelength and highest frequency of all EM waves. They originate from changes in the nucleus of an atom — typically from radioactive decay. Gamma rays are the most penetrating type of EM radiation, passing through most materials including body tissue and thin metal sheets. Only thick lead or several metres of concrete can significantly reduce their intensity.

Uses of gamma rays include: sterilising medical instruments and food (killing bacteria without heat), treating cancer through radiotherapy (focused beams destroy tumour cells), and as a medical tracer when a patient is injected with a gamma-emitting substance so doctors can track its path through the body. Because gamma rays are strongly ionising, overexposure can cause cell damage, mutations, radiation sickness, and cancer.

Key Fact

All EM waves travel at the same speed in a vacuum (3 × 108 m/s), but they differ in wavelength and frequency. The higher the frequency, the more energy the wave carries — this is why gamma rays are more dangerous than radio waves.

Radio waves: TV, radio broadcasts, Bluetooth, Wi-Fi. Danger: No significant danger at normal exposure levels.

Microwaves: Satellite communication, mobile phones, cooking food. Danger: Internal heating of body tissue if absorbed (though levels from phones are very low).

Infrared: Heaters, thermal cameras, remote controls, cooking. Danger: Skin burns from excessive exposure.

Visible light: Vision, photography, fibre optics. Danger: Eye damage from very intense sources (e.g. lasers, looking directly at the Sun).

Ultraviolet: Fluorescent lamps, detecting forgeries, sterilisation, vitamin D production. Danger: Sunburn, premature ageing, skin cancer, cataracts.

X-rays: Medical imaging, security scanners, CT scans. Danger: Cell damage and increased cancer risk (ionising).

Gamma rays: Sterilisation, cancer treatment (radiotherapy), medical tracers. Danger: Cell damage, mutations, cancer, radiation sickness (most ionising).
lessons.exam_tip_html: In Physics Paper 2, you will often be asked to compare different EM waves or link a specific wave type to its uses and dangers. Always state whether the wave is ionising or non-ionising, name a specific use with a brief explanation of how it works, and identify the hazard. For “explain” questions, make sure you connect the property (e.g. short wavelength, high penetration) to the use or danger — do not just list facts. For calculation questions using v = f × λ, remember that all EM waves in a vacuum travel at 3 × 108 m/s.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • All EM waves are transverse, travel at 3 × 108 m/s in a vacuum, and differ only in wavelength and frequency. The spectrum runs: radio → microwave → infrared → visible → ultraviolet → X-ray → gamma.
  • Each type has specific uses linked to its properties — e.g. X-rays penetrate soft tissue (medical imaging), infrared is emitted by warm objects (thermal cameras), radio waves diffract around obstacles (broadcasting).
  • UV, X-rays, and gamma rays are ionising — they can damage cells and DNA, increasing cancer risk. Know the precautions for each.

lessons.title: Magnets, Electromagnetism and the Motor Effect
lessons.description: Permanent and induced magnets, magnetic fields, electromagnets, and how the motor effect works.
lessons.content_html:
Magnetism as a Non-Contact Force

magnetism is a non-contact force — it acts at a distance without objects touching. Unlike gravity, which acts between all masses, magnetism only acts between three types of object: permanent magnets, induced magnets, and electromagnets. Only certain materials are magnetic: iron, steel, nickel, and cobalt.

Every magnet has two poles — a north pole and a south pole. The poles are where the magnetic field is strongest. When two magnets are brought together, like poles repel and unlike poles attract. If you hang a bar magnet on a string so it can spin freely, its north pole will point towards geographic north — this is how a compass works.

Key Fact

Like poles repel. Unlike poles attract. The poles are where the magnetic forces are strongest.

Permanent and Induced Magnets

A permanent magnet produces its own magnetic field all the time. It does not need electricity or another magnet to work. Bar magnets, horseshoe magnets, and fridge magnets are all permanent magnets. Steel is used to make permanent magnets because it does not lose its magnetism easily.

An induced magnet is a magnetic material that becomes magnetised only when it is placed inside a magnetic field. For example, bringing a permanent magnet close to an iron nail turns the nail into a temporary magnet. The induced magnet’s poles always line up so that the nearest pole is opposite to the permanent magnet’s pole — this means induced magnets are always attracted to the permanent magnet, never repelled.

Steel retains its magnetism when removed from a magnetic field, making it ideal for permanent magnets. Iron magnetises more strongly than steel but loses its magnetism quickly once removed from the field — this makes iron better for temporary or induced magnets. Electromagnets use an iron core precisely because the magnetism must switch on and off with the current.

Magnetic Field Lines

A magnetic field is the region around a magnet where a magnetic force acts. We represent it using field lines. These lines always run from the north pole to the south pole outside the magnet. Where the lines are close together the field is strong; where they spread apart the field is weak.

You can reveal field lines by sprinkling iron filings around a bar magnet or by tracing the direction a plotting compass needle points as you move it around the magnet. Two unlike poles placed near each other produce field lines that curve between them (attraction). Two like poles produce lines that push away from each other (repulsion).

Key Fact

Magnetic field lines always point from north to south. Closer lines mean a stronger field. The field is strongest at the poles.

Electromagnets

When an electric current flows through a wire, it produces a magnetic field around the wire. The field lines form concentric circles centred on the wire. If you increase the current, the field gets stronger. Reversing the current reverses the direction of the field.

Winding the wire into a coil called a solenoid concentrates the magnetic field. Inside a solenoid, the field lines are parallel and evenly spaced — this is a uniform magnetic field. The field pattern around a solenoid looks very similar to the field around a bar magnet, with a north pole at one end and a south pole at the other.

Adding an iron core inside a solenoid creates an electromagnet. The iron core becomes an induced magnet and greatly increases the field strength. Three ways to make an electromagnet stronger are: increase the current, add more turns of wire, or use a softer iron core. When the current is switched off, the iron core loses its magnetism almost immediately — this is what makes electromagnets so useful.

Electromagnets are used in scrapyard cranes (pick up and drop steel cars by switching the current on and off), circuit breakers (an excessive current magnetises a coil which trips a switch to break the circuit), electric bells (the electromagnet attracts an iron armature to strike the bell, then the circuit breaks and the process repeats), and relays (a small current in one circuit activates an electromagnet that closes a switch in a separate, higher-power circuit).

The Motor Effect

When a conductor carrying a current is placed inside a magnetic field, it experiences a force. This is called the motor effect. The force acts at right angles to both the direction of the current and the direction of the magnetic field. If either the current or the magnetic field is reversed, the direction of the force reverses too.

The size of the force depends on three factors: the magnetic flux density (how strong the field is, measured in tesla, T), the current through the conductor (in amps, A), and the length of the conductor inside the field (in metres, m). The equation is:

Key Fact

\(Force = \text{magnetic flux density} \times current \times length\)
F = B × I × l
where F is in newtons (N), B is in tesla (T), I is in amps (A), and l is in metres (m).

Fleming’s Left-Hand Rule

Fleming’s left-hand rule tells you the direction of the force (and therefore the direction of motion). Hold your left hand with the thumb, first finger, and second finger all at right angles to each other:

First finger — direction of the magnetic Field (north to south). Second finger — direction of the Current (positive to negative). Thumb — direction of Motion (the force on the conductor).

Step 1: Identify the direction of the magnetic field (from north to south pole of the magnets). Step 2: Identify the direction of the current (conventional current flows from positive to negative). Step 3: Point your left hand’s first finger in the field direction and your second finger in the current direction. Step 4: Your thumb now points in the direction the wire will move. If the question gives two of the three directions, use the rule to find the third.

Electric Motors

An electric motor uses the motor effect to produce continuous rotation. A rectangular coil of wire sits between the poles of two permanent magnets. When current flows through the coil, the two sides of the coil experience forces in opposite directions (one side is pushed up, the other is pushed down), creating a turning effect.

The coil would stop after half a turn because the forces would then act to push it back the other way. To prevent this, a split-ring commutator reverses the direction of the current every half turn. This means the forces always push the same side of the coil in the same direction, keeping it spinning continuously. Carbon brushes maintain electrical contact with the spinning commutator.

Key Fact

Three ways to make an electric motor spin faster: increase the current, use a stronger magnet (greater magnetic flux density), or add more turns of wire to the coil.

The key components are: a rectangular coil of insulated wire mounted on an axle so it can rotate, two permanent magnets with opposite poles facing each other to create a uniform field, a split-ring commutator attached to the coil that reverses the current direction every half turn, and carbon brushes that press against the commutator to connect the coil to the power supply. The coil rotates because the two sides experience forces in opposite directions due to the motor effect.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For calculation questions using F = B × I × l, always show your working: write out the formula, substitute values with units, and calculate. If you need to rearrange, use the formula triangle. For “Explain” questions about the motor effect or electric motors, state the physics rule first (e.g. “a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field experiences a force”), then explain each step of the process in order. When asked about Fleming’s left-hand rule, always state which finger represents which quantity — field, current, and motion.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Permanent magnets produce their own field; induced magnets only become magnetic inside an external field and are always attracted to the permanent magnet.
  • An electromagnet is a solenoid with an iron core — its strength depends on current, number of turns, and the core material. It can be switched on and off.
  • The motor effect (F = B × I × l) describes the force on a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field, and Fleming’s left-hand rule gives the direction of that force. A split-ring commutator keeps a DC motor spinning continuously.

lessons.title: Moments, Levers, Gears and Momentum Changes
lessons.description: Calculating moments and understanding how levers, gears and safety features use force and momentum.
lessons.content_html:
Moments and the Turning Effect of Forces

When you push a door open, you apply a force at a distance from the hinge. The door swings because your push creates a moment. A moment is the turning effect of a force around a fixed point called a pivot.

Key Fact

The moment of a force is calculated using: \(moment (Nm) = force (N) \times \text{distance from pivot} (m)\), or \(M = F \times d\). The distance must be measured perpendicular to the direction of the force.

The unit of a moment is the newton metre (Nm). A larger force or a greater distance from the pivot both produce a larger moment. This is why it is easier to open a door by pushing near the handle (far from the hinge) than by pushing close to the hinge.

A child with a weight of 420 N sits 1.6 m from the pivot of a see-saw. Calculate the moment of the force.

\(M = F \times d\) = 420 × 1.6 = 672 Nm

Always check that the distance is in metres. If you are given 20 cm, convert to 0.2 m before substituting into the equation.

Balancing Moments — The Principle of Moments

When an object is balanced (in equilibrium), the total clockwise moments about the pivot equal the total anticlockwise moments. This is the principle of moments.

On a balanced see-saw, if a heavier child sits closer to the pivot and a lighter child sits further away, the moments can be equal. You can use this principle to find an unknown force or distance:

\(F_{1} \times d_{1} = F_{2} \times d_{2}\)

Levers

A lever is a simple machine that multiplies the effect of a force. It consists of a rigid bar that turns around a pivot. By applying a small effort force at a large distance from the pivot, you can move a heavy load that is close to the pivot.

Everyday examples include crowbars, wheelbarrows, scissors, and spanners. A builder using a crowbar applies a force at the long end to lift a heavy floorboard at the short end — the long lever arm means a smaller force is needed to create the same moment.

Gears

A gear is a toothed wheel that meshes with another toothed wheel. Gears transmit the turning effect of a force from one part of a machine to another.

Key Fact

When a small gear drives a large gear, the large gear turns more slowly but with a greater moment (turning force). When a large gear drives a small gear, the small gear turns faster but with a smaller moment. Gears that mesh always turn in opposite directions.

Gears are used in bicycles, cars and clocks. A low gear on a bicycle uses a large rear gear driven by the pedals, giving a greater turning force at the wheel — useful for climbing hills. A high gear uses a smaller rear gear, giving less force but more speed on flat roads.

Momentum

Momentum is a measure of how difficult it is to stop a moving object. It depends on both mass and velocity:

\(momentum (kg m/s) = mass (kg) \times velocity (m/s)\), or \(p = m \times v\)

A heavy lorry travelling at 3 m/s has a momentum of 10,000 × 3 = 30,000 kg m/s. A bullet has much less mass, but its very high velocity gives it a large momentum too. Momentum is a vector quantity — it has both size and direction.

Force and the Rate of Change of Momentum

When a force acts on an object, the object’s momentum changes. The faster the momentum changes, the greater the force involved. This relationship is expressed as:

\(force (N) = \text{change in momentum} (kg m/s) \div time (s)\), or \(F = \Delta p / t\)

Key Fact

A fast change in momentum produces a large force, which can cause serious injury. A slow change in momentum produces a smaller force. This is why safety features are designed to increase the time over which momentum changes during a collision.

A person of mass 71 kg is in a car travelling at 25 m/s. The car crashes and stops.

Step 1 — Calculate momentum: p = m × v = 71 × 25 = 1,775 kg m/s

Step 2 — With crumple zones (crash time 0.54 s): F = 1,775 ÷ 0.54 = 3,287 N

Step 3 — Without crumple zones (crash time 0.35 s): F = 1,775 ÷ 0.35 = 5,071 N

The crumple zones reduce the force on the person by about 35% because the collision time is longer.

Safety Features in Vehicles

Modern vehicles include several features that protect occupants by increasing the time over which momentum changes, thereby reducing the force experienced:

  • Crumple zones — the front and rear of the car are designed to crumple and deform during a collision. This absorbs kinetic energy and extends the time of impact.
  • Seatbelts — stretch slightly during a crash, increasing the time it takes for the person to decelerate and spreading the force across the chest.
  • Air bags — inflate rapidly and then deflate as the person pushes into them, increasing the time of deceleration and cushioning the impact on the head and chest.

The change in momentum in a crash is fixed — the person goes from moving to stationary. Since F = Δp / t, if the time (t) increases, the force (F) must decrease for the same change in momentum (Δp). Every safety feature works on this principle: absorb the impact over a longer period to reduce the peak force on the body.
lessons.exam_tip_html: In calculation questions on moments, always check units — convert centimetres to metres before substituting. For questions on vehicle safety, explain how the feature increases the time of impact and state that this reduces the force (F = Δp / t). Examiners want both parts for full marks. If asked to “compare” two situations, calculate both values and write a concluding sentence stating which is greater and why.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • A moment is the turning effect of a force: M = F × d. Levers and gears use moments to multiply forces.
  • Momentum (p = mv) describes how hard it is to stop a moving object. Force equals the rate of change of momentum: F = Δp / t.
  • Vehicle safety features (crumple zones, seatbelts, air bags) increase the collision time to reduce the force on occupants.
