lessons.title: Reflection, Sound Waves and Waves for Detection
lessons.description: The law of reflection, sound wave properties, ultrasound applications, and seismic wave evidence for Earth's structure.
lessons.content_html:
The Law of Reflection

When a wave hits a boundary between two different materials, it can be reflected, transmitted, or absorbed. Reflection is when the wave bounces back from the surface. This applies to all types of waves — light, sound, and water waves all follow the same rules.

To describe reflection precisely, scientists use a set of standard terms. The normal is an imaginary line drawn at 90° (perpendicular) to the reflecting surface at the point where the wave hits. The incoming wave is called the incident ray, and the wave that bounces back is the reflected ray.

The angle of incidence is measured between the incident ray and the normal. The angle of reflection is measured between the reflected ray and the normal. Both angles are always measured from the normal — not from the surface of the mirror.

Key Fact

The law of reflection states that the angle of incidence always equals the angle of reflection. This is true for every type of wave at every surface.

In the exam, you may need to construct ray diagrams. Draw the mirror as a straight line, then draw the normal at 90° to the mirror at the point where the ray hits. Mark the incident ray coming in and the reflected ray going out. Use a protractor to check that the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection.

Smooth surfaces (like a flat mirror) produce specular reflection. The reflected rays are all parallel, so a clear image is formed. This is why you can see your reflection in a mirror or in still water.

Rough surfaces scatter reflected waves in all directions. This is called diffuse reflection. Each tiny part of the surface still obeys the law of reflection, but because the surface is uneven, the reflected rays go in many different directions. No clear image is formed.

An image formed in a plane mirror is virtual (cannot be projected onto a screen), upright (not upside down), and laterally inverted (left and right are swapped). This is why the word “AMBULANCE” is written backwards on the front of ambulances — so it reads correctly in a driver’s rear-view mirror.

Sound Waves

Sound is produced when an object vibrates. These vibrations travel through a medium (solid, liquid, or gas) as a longitudinal wave. In a longitudinal wave, the particles vibrate back and forth parallel to the direction the wave travels, creating areas of compression (high pressure) and rarefaction (low pressure).

Sound waves are mechanical waves — they need a medium to travel through. Sound cannot travel through a vacuum. This can be demonstrated using a bell jar experiment: as air is pumped out, the sound of a ringing bell fades until it becomes inaudible, even though the bell is still vibrating.

Sound travels at different speeds through different materials. It travels fastest through solids (particles are closest together), slower through liquids, and slowest through gases. In air at room temperature, the speed of sound is approximately 330 m/s.

Key Fact

The range of normal human hearing is 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz (20 kHz). Sounds below 20 Hz are called infrasound. Sounds above 20,000 Hz are called ultrasound.

When sound waves enter the ear, they cause the eardrum to vibrate. These vibrations are passed through the tiny ear bones to the inner ear, where they are converted into electrical signals sent to the brain. The eardrum and ear bones can only vibrate at certain rates, which is why our hearing is limited to the 20 Hz–20,000 Hz range.

The pitch of a sound depends on its frequency — a higher frequency means a higher pitch. The loudness of a sound depends on its amplitude — a larger amplitude means a louder sound. On an oscilloscope trace, higher pitch appears as waves closer together, and louder sound appears as taller waves.

An echo is a reflection of sound. When sound waves hit a hard, smooth surface (such as a cliff face or the wall of a cave), they bounce back and can be heard again after a short delay. Soft, rough surfaces absorb sound rather than reflecting it — this is why cinemas have padded walls and curtains to prevent echoes that would spoil the film audio.

Echo calculations are common in exams. Remember that the sound wave travels there and back, so the distance to the reflecting surface is half the total distance the sound travels. Use the equation: distance = speed × time, then divide by 2.

Ultrasound and Its Uses

Ultrasound refers to sound waves with frequencies above 20,000 Hz — beyond the upper limit of human hearing. Despite being inaudible to humans, ultrasound has many practical applications because of the way it reflects at boundaries between materials of different densities.

Key Fact

When ultrasound waves reach a boundary between two media with different densities, they are partly reflected back. A detector measures the time between the ultrasound pulse leaving the source and the reflection arriving back. This time is used to calculate the depth of the boundary.

Medical imaging: Ultrasound is widely used in pre-natal scanning to check that a foetus is developing normally. The ultrasound waves are partly reflected at the boundaries between different tissues (skin, muscle, bone, fluid). A computer combines many readings to build a detailed image. Ultrasound is preferred over X-rays for this purpose because it is non-invasive, considered safe (it does not cause cell damage like ionising radiation), and provides real-time images.

Echo sounding and SONAR (Sound Navigation and Ranging): Ships and submarines send pulses of ultrasound towards the sea floor. The pulses reflect off the bottom and return to a detector on the vessel. By measuring the time taken for the pulse to return and knowing the speed of sound in water, the depth can be calculated. SONAR is also used to detect submarines, shoals of fish, and underwater obstacles. Bats and dolphins use a natural version of this — they emit ultrasound and listen for the echoes to navigate and locate prey.

A submarine sends an ultrasound pulse to the sea floor. The pulse returns 0.35 s later. The speed of sound in water is 1,600 m/s.

Step 1: Total distance = speed × time = 1,600 × 0.35 = 560 m.
Step 2: The pulse travels to the sea floor and back, so divide by 2: 560 ÷ 2 = 280 m.
The sea floor is 280 m below the submarine.

Seismic Waves and the Structure of the Earth

Earthquakes produce seismic waves that travel through the Earth. By studying how these waves travel, scientists have been able to work out the internal structure of the Earth — something that cannot be observed directly. There are two main types of seismic wave.

P-waves (primary waves) are longitudinal waves. They cause the ground to vibrate in the same direction the wave is travelling. P-waves can travel through both solids and liquids, so they can pass through all layers of the Earth — the crust, mantle, outer core, and inner core. They are the fastest seismic waves and arrive at detection stations first.

S-waves (secondary waves) are transverse waves. They cause the ground to vibrate at right angles to the direction of travel. S-waves can only travel through solids — they cannot pass through liquids. This means S-waves are blocked by the Earth’s liquid outer core.

Key Fact

The fact that S-waves cannot travel through the outer core proves it is liquid. P-waves can travel through the outer core but change direction at the boundaries between layers. Together, the behaviour of P-waves and S-waves provides evidence that the Earth has a solid inner core, a liquid outer core, and a solid mantle (which behaves like a solid despite being able to flow very slowly).

Both types of seismic wave change speed as they travel deeper into the Earth because the density of the rock increases. This causes the waves to follow curved paths through the mantle. When they reach a boundary between layers of different density or state, they change direction suddenly — this is refraction. By mapping where P-waves and S-waves are detected on the Earth’s surface, scientists can work out the size and state of each internal layer.

After an earthquake, seismometers around the world detect the arriving waves. There is a large “shadow zone” on the far side of the Earth where no S-waves are detected at all. This shadow zone shows that the outer core is liquid, because S-waves cannot pass through liquid. P-waves are also refracted at the core–mantle boundary, creating their own shadow zone, but they do eventually reach the far side after being bent through the core.

These observations allowed scientists to discover that the Earth has a thin crust (10–100 km thick), a thick mantle that behaves as a solid, a liquid outer core made mainly of iron and nickel, and a solid inner core. Without seismic wave studies, this internal structure would remain unknown.
lessons.exam_tip_html: In questions on waves for detection and exploration, always state the type of wave (longitudinal or transverse), the medium it can or cannot travel through, and the evidence this provides. For echo and SONAR calculations, remember the sound travels there and back — divide the total distance by 2. When drawing ray diagrams, label the normal, incident ray, reflected ray, and both angles carefully using a protractor.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The law of reflection states that the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection — both measured from the normal. Smooth surfaces give specular reflection; rough surfaces scatter waves.
  • Sound is a longitudinal, mechanical wave. Human hearing ranges from 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz. Ultrasound (above 20 kHz) is used in medical imaging and SONAR by detecting reflected pulses.
  • Seismic P-waves (longitudinal, travel through solids and liquids) and S-waves (transverse, solids only) provide evidence for the Earth’s layered structure — including proof that the outer core is liquid.

lessons.title: Lenses, Visible Light and Black Body Radiation
lessons.description: Convex and concave lenses, colour filters, and black body radiation.
lessons.content_html:
Lenses and Refraction

A lens forms an image by refracting light. When light passes from air into glass it slows down, and when it leaves the glass it speeds up again. The curved surfaces of a lens bend the light in a controlled way, either bringing rays together or spreading them apart.

There are two key terms you must know for ray diagrams. The principal focus (also called the focal point, F) is the point where parallel rays of light either converge or appear to diverge from after passing through the lens. The focal length is the distance from the centre of the lens to the principal focus.

Convex (Converging) Lenses

A convex lens is thickest at the centre. It refracts parallel rays of light inwards so that they converge and meet at the principal focus on the other side of the lens. This is why convex lenses are also called converging lenses.

The type of image a convex lens produces depends on where the object is placed relative to the focal point. If the object is beyond the focal point (further from the lens than F), the lens produces a real image. A real image is formed where the refracted rays actually meet, and it can be captured on a screen. Real images are always inverted (upside down). Cameras and projectors use convex lenses in this way.

If the object is placed between the focal point and the lens (closer than F), the refracted rays diverge. They appear to come from a point on the same side as the object, producing a virtual image. A virtual image is upright, magnified, and cannot be projected onto a screen. This is how a magnifying glass works.

Key Fact

Convex lens images: Object beyond F → real, inverted image (can be on a screen). Object between F and the lens → virtual, upright, magnified image (magnifying glass).

Concave (Diverging) Lenses

A concave lens is thinnest at the centre. It refracts parallel rays of light outwards so they spread apart. If you trace the diverging rays back, they appear to come from a single point on the same side as the incoming light — this is the principal focus of a concave lens.

A concave lens always produces a virtual image, no matter where the object is placed. The image is always upright, smaller than the object, and on the same side as the object. Concave lenses are used in spectacles to correct short-sightedness (myopia).

For a convex lens, draw two rays from the top of the object: (1) a ray parallel to the principal axis that refracts through the focal point on the other side, and (2) a ray through the centre of the lens that continues straight. Where the two refracted rays meet is the top of the image.

For a concave lens, draw: (1) a ray parallel to the principal axis that refracts and appears to come from the focal point on the same side as the incoming light, and (2) a ray through the centre of the lens that continues straight. Trace the diverging rays back with dashed lines to find the virtual image.

Magnification

Magnification tells you how much bigger or smaller the image is compared to the object. It is calculated using the equation:

\(magnification = \text{image height} \div \text{object height}\)

Magnification is a ratio, so it has no units. Both heights must be measured in the same unit (mm or cm). A magnification greater than 1 means the image is larger than the object; less than 1 means it is smaller.

Key Fact

Magnification equation: magnification = image height ÷ object height. This is a ratio with no units. A magnification of 5 means the image is 5 times larger than the real object.

Visible Light and Colour

Visible light is a small part of the electromagnetic spectrum. It is the only part that human eyes can detect. The visible spectrum ranges from red (longest wavelength, about 700 nm) to violet (shortest wavelength, about 400 nm), with the colours blending smoothly into each other — they do not have sharp boundaries.

The colour of an opaque object depends on which wavelengths of light it reflects and which it absorbs. A red jumper reflects red light and absorbs all other colours. A white object reflects all wavelengths equally, while a black object absorbs all wavelengths.

A colour filter works by absorbing certain wavelengths of light and transmitting others. A red filter absorbs all colours except red, so only red light passes through. A blue filter transmits only blue light.

When you view a coloured object under coloured light, the object can only reflect the colours present in the light. A red shirt under red light still looks red (it reflects the red light). But a red shirt under blue light looks black — there is no red light to reflect, and it absorbs the blue light.

Transparent objects transmit all light through them (e.g. clear glass). Translucent objects transmit some light but scatter it, so you cannot see clearly through them (e.g. frosted glass). Opaque objects do not transmit any light.

Specular reflection occurs when light reflects off a smooth surface (such as a mirror or still water). All the reflected rays travel in the same direction, producing a clear reflected image.

Diffuse reflection occurs when light hits a rough surface (such as paper or fabric). The reflected rays scatter in many different directions, so no clear image is formed. Most objects around us cause diffuse reflection.

Black Body Radiation

All objects, no matter what their temperature, continuously emit and absorb infrared radiation. The hotter an object is, the more infrared radiation it emits in a given time. This is why you can feel the warmth radiating from a hot radiator or a bonfire even without touching it.

A perfect black body is defined as an object that absorbs all of the radiation incident upon it. It does not reflect or transmit any radiation. Because a good absorber is also a good emitter, a perfect black body is also the best possible emitter of radiation at any given temperature.

Key Fact

A perfect black body absorbs all radiation falling on it and emits radiation at the maximum possible rate for its temperature. Dark, matt surfaces are better absorbers and emitters than light, shiny surfaces.

As the temperature of an object increases, the intensity of radiation emitted at every wavelength increases. However, the intensity of shorter wavelengths increases more rapidly. This is why very hot objects (such as stars) shift from glowing red to orange, yellow, white, and eventually blue-white as they get hotter.

An object is in thermal equilibrium when the rate at which it absorbs radiation equals the rate at which it emits radiation — its temperature stays constant. If an object absorbs radiation faster than it emits it, the temperature rises. If it emits faster than it absorbs, the temperature falls.

The temperature of the Earth depends on the balance between energy absorbed from the Sun, energy reflected back into space, and energy emitted by the Earth into space. Changes to the atmosphere (such as increased greenhouse gases) can alter this balance and affect the Earth’s temperature.

For magnification calculations, always show your working and state that magnification has no units. Black body radiation questions may ask you to explain why a dark surface cools faster than a shiny one, or to describe how the Earth’s temperature is maintained — link your answer to the balance between absorption and emission of radiation.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Convex lenses converge light and can produce real (inverted) or virtual (upright, magnified) images depending on object position. Concave lenses diverge light and always produce virtual, upright, smaller images.
  • The colour of an opaque object depends on which wavelengths it reflects — colour filters absorb certain wavelengths and transmit others.
  • All objects emit and absorb infrared radiation. A perfect black body absorbs all incident radiation and is the best emitter. The Earth’s temperature depends on the balance between absorbed and emitted radiation.

lessons.title: Electromagnetic Induction and Transformers
lessons.description: How moving conductors and changing fields induce potential, and how transformers change voltage.
lessons.content_html:
The Generator Effect

The generator effect is the reverse of the motor effect. Instead of using a current to produce motion, motion is used to produce a current. When a wire or coil moves through a magnetic field — or when a magnetic field moves past a stationary conductor — a potential difference is induced across the ends of the conductor. If the conductor is part of a complete circuit, this induced potential difference drives a current.

This process is called electromagnetic induction. It is the principle behind all generators, whether they power a bicycle light or a national power station.

Key Fact

An induced potential difference is produced when there is relative movement between a conductor and a magnetic field. It does not matter which one moves — what matters is that the magnetic field lines being “cut” by the conductor are changing.

Factors Affecting the Induced Potential Difference

The size of the induced potential difference can be increased in three ways:

1. Increasing the speed of movement — moving the conductor or magnet faster means more field lines are cut per second, producing a larger voltage. 2. Increasing the strength of the magnetic field — a stronger field means more flux is available to be cut. 3. Increasing the number of turns on the coil — each turn of wire contributes its own induced voltage, so more turns means a higher total output.

The direction of the induced current can be reversed by either reversing the direction of movement or reversing the polarity of the magnetic field. If both are reversed at the same time, the current direction stays the same.

A simple demonstration uses a bar magnet pushed into and out of a solenoid connected to a sensitive ammeter (galvanometer). As the magnet enters, the ammeter needle deflects one way. As it is removed, the needle deflects the opposite way. When the magnet is stationary inside the coil, there is no deflection because the field is not changing. Moving the magnet faster produces a larger deflection.

Alternators and Dynamos

An alternator is a generator that produces alternating current (a.c.). Inside an alternator, a coil of wire rotates between the poles of a magnet. As the coil spins, each side of the coil alternately moves up and then down through the field, so the direction of the induced current reverses every half-turn. The coil is connected to the external circuit by slip rings and carbon brushes, which maintain a continuous but reversing connection.

A dynamo produces direct current (d.c.). Its construction is almost identical to an alternator, but instead of slip rings it uses a split-ring commutator. The commutator swaps the connections to the external circuit every half-turn, so although the current in the coil reverses, the current in the external circuit always flows in the same direction.

Key Fact

Alternator = slip rings = a.c. output. Dynamo = split-ring commutator = d.c. output. This is the key difference the exam tests. Alternators are used in power stations and cars; dynamos are used in some bicycle lights.

Microphones and Loudspeakers

Microphones and loudspeakers are practical applications of electromagnetic induction and the motor effect working in reverse.

In a moving-coil microphone, sound waves hit a diaphragm, causing it to vibrate. Attached to the diaphragm is a coil of wire that sits inside a permanent magnet’s field. As the diaphragm vibrates, the coil moves back and forth within the magnetic field, and an alternating potential difference is induced across the coil. The frequency of this a.c. signal matches the frequency of the incoming sound wave, which is how sound is converted into an electrical signal.

A loudspeaker works in the opposite way. An alternating current is fed into a coil of wire (the voice coil) that sits in a permanent magnetic field. The changing current causes the coil to experience a force that alternates in direction (the motor effect), making the coil vibrate back and forth. The coil is attached to a cone, which pushes and pulls the surrounding air to produce sound waves. The frequency of the a.c. signal determines the pitch of the sound produced.

Microphone: Sound → diaphragm vibrates → coil moves in magnetic field → a.c. induced (generator effect). Converts sound energy into electrical energy.

Loudspeaker: a.c. signal → coil in magnetic field experiences alternating force → cone vibrates → sound produced (motor effect). Converts electrical energy into sound energy.

Both contain the same core components — a coil, a permanent magnet, and a diaphragm or cone — but the energy transfer is reversed.

Transformers

A transformer is a device that changes the potential difference (voltage) of an a.c. supply. Transformers only work with alternating current because they rely on a continuously changing magnetic field.

A transformer consists of two coils of insulated wire — the primary coil and the secondary coil — wound around a shared iron core. The a.c. in the primary coil creates a changing magnetic field in the iron core. This changing field passes through the secondary coil and induces an alternating potential difference across it. The iron core is made of soft iron because it magnetises and demagnetises easily, efficiently transferring the changing field.

Key Fact

Transformers only work with a.c. (not d.c.) because a direct current produces a steady magnetic field, which does not change and therefore cannot induce a potential difference in the secondary coil.

Step-Up and Step-Down Transformers

A step-up transformer increases the potential difference. It has more turns on the secondary coil than on the primary coil. A step-down transformer decreases the potential difference. It has fewer turns on the secondary coil than on the primary coil.

The relationship between the voltages and the number of turns is given by the turns ratio equation:

\(V_{p} / V_{s} = n_{p} / n_{s}\)

Where Vp is the potential difference across the primary coil, Vs is the potential difference across the secondary coil, np is the number of turns on the primary coil, and ns is the number of turns on the secondary coil.

A step-down transformer has 2000 turns on the primary coil and 100 turns on the secondary coil. The input voltage is 400 V. Calculate the output voltage.

Step 1: Write the equation: Vp / Vs = np / ns

Step 2: Substitute: 400 / Vs = 2000 / 100

Step 3: Rearrange: Vs = 400 × 100 / 2000 = 20 V

Transformers in the National Grid

The National Grid uses step-up and step-down transformers to transmit electricity efficiently across the country. Power stations generate electricity at around 25,000 V. Step-up transformers at the power station increase this to 400,000 V for transmission through overhead cables. Near homes and businesses, step-down transformers reduce the voltage back to 230 V for safe domestic use.

Transmitting at high voltage means the current is kept low (since power = voltage × current, and power stays the same). A lower current means less energy is wasted as heat in the cables, making the system more efficient. Without transformers, huge amounts of energy would be lost during transmission.

Power transferred = voltage × current (P = V × I). For a fixed power, increasing voltage decreases current. The power wasted as heat in the cables = current² × resistance (P = I² × R). Since wasted power depends on current squared, even a small reduction in current dramatically reduces energy loss. This is why the National Grid transmits at 400,000 V — the current is very small, so very little energy is lost as heat.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Transformer calculation questions are very common in the exam. Always start by writing out the equation Vp / Vs = np / ns, then substitute and rearrange. For “explain” questions about the National Grid, link three ideas in a chain: step-up transformer increases voltage → this decreases current → less energy wasted as heat (P = I²R). For questions comparing alternators and dynamos, always name the specific component that differs: slip rings vs split-ring commutator.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Electromagnetic induction occurs when a conductor moves through a magnetic field (or vice versa), inducing a potential difference — increased by faster movement, stronger fields, or more coil turns.
  • Alternators use slip rings to produce a.c.; dynamos use a split-ring commutator to produce d.c. Microphones use the generator effect; loudspeakers use the motor effect.
  • Transformers change a.c. voltage using the turns ratio Vp/Vs = np/ns. The National Grid uses step-up transformers (high V, low I) to reduce energy loss in transmission cables.

lessons.title: Space Physics: The Solar System and Beyond
lessons.description: Our solar system, the life cycle of stars, orbital motion, and evidence for the expanding universe.
lessons.content_html:
Our Solar System

Our solar system consists of the Sun at its centre, orbited by eight planets, dwarf planets, moons, asteroids and comets. The Sun is a main sequence star — a medium-sized star that has been fusing hydrogen into helium for about 4.6 billion years. Everything in the solar system is held in orbit by the Sun’s gravitational pull.

The eight planets, in order from the Sun, are Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune. The first four are rocky planets (smaller, solid surfaces), while the outer four are gas giants (much larger, mostly gas and liquid). Beyond Neptune lies a region of dwarf planets including Pluto.

Key Fact

The solar system formed about 4.6 billion years ago from a collapsing cloud of dust and gas called a nebula. Gravity pulled material together to form the Sun, while leftover material clumped together to form the planets and other objects.

Orbits in the Solar System

All planets orbit the Sun in slightly elliptical (oval-shaped) paths. Moons orbit planets in a similar way. gravity provides the centripetal force needed to keep an object moving in a curved path — without it, a planet would fly off in a straight line. The closer a planet is to the Sun, the stronger the gravitational pull and the faster it orbits.

A satellite is any object that orbits a planet or star. Satellites can be natural (like the Moon) or artificial (like the International Space Station). Artificial satellites orbit Earth at different heights depending on their purpose.

Natural satellites are objects that orbit planets due to gravity alone. The Moon is Earth’s only natural satellite, but Jupiter has at least 95 known moons.

Artificial satellites are human-made objects placed into orbit for specific purposes. Communications satellites sit in geostationary orbit (high altitude, 24-hour period, stays above the same point). Weather satellites use low polar orbits to scan the entire Earth.

The Life Cycle of Stars

Stars do not last forever. They are born, they live, and they die — and the way a star dies depends on its mass.

Birth of a Star

All stars begin as a nebula — a vast cloud of hydrogen gas and dust. Gravity pulls the gas together, and as the cloud contracts it heats up. The contracting ball of gas is called a protostar. When the core reaches around 15 million °C, nuclear fusion begins — hydrogen nuclei fuse to form helium, releasing enormous energy. Once fusion is stable, the star becomes a main sequence star.

Key Fact

A main sequence star is in a stable phase where the outward pressure from nuclear fusion is balanced by the inward pull of gravity. This balance is called hydrostatic equilibrium and can last for billions of years. Our Sun is currently a main sequence star.

Death of a Star — Sun-Sized Stars

When a Sun-sized star runs out of hydrogen fuel, the core contracts while the outer layers expand and cool, turning it into a red giant. The red giant sheds its outer layers into space, forming a planetary nebula. The remaining core collapses to form a white dwarf — an incredibly dense remnant about the size of Earth that slowly cools and fades.

Death of a Star — Massive Stars

Stars much larger than the Sun follow a more dramatic path. After the main sequence phase, a massive star swells into a red supergiant. When the core runs out of fuel, it collapses violently, triggering an explosion called a supernova. A supernova briefly outshines an entire galaxy and blasts heavy elements (iron, gold, uranium) into space.

What remains after the supernova depends on the original mass of the star:

  • Neutron star — if the remaining core is between about 1.4 and 3 solar masses, it collapses into a neutron star. Neutron stars are incredibly dense — a teaspoon of neutron star material would weigh about a billion tonnes on Earth.
  • Black hole — if the remaining core is above about 3 solar masses, gravity is so strong that nothing can stop the collapse. The core forms a black hole, a region of space where gravity is so intense that not even light can escape.

Sun-sized stars: Nebula → Protostar → Main sequence star → Red giant → Planetary nebula → White dwarf. The process is relatively gentle — no explosion occurs. The white dwarf slowly cools and fades over billions of years.

Massive stars: Nebula → Protostar → Main sequence star → Red supergiant → Supernova → Neutron star or Black hole. The supernova is one of the most energetic events in the universe. The heavy elements scattered by supernovae eventually form new stars, planets and even living things — we are literally made of stardust.

Key Fact

Elements heavier than iron can only be created during a supernova. Every atom of gold, silver and uranium on Earth was forged in the explosion of a massive star billions of years ago.

Red-Shift and the Expanding Universe

When astronomers analysed the absorption spectra of distant galaxies, they found the dark lines were shifted towards the red end of the spectrum. This effect is called red-shift.

Red-shift happens because the galaxy is moving away from us. As the galaxy recedes, the light waves are stretched out, increasing their wavelength and shifting them towards the red end of the spectrum. This is similar to how the pitch of an ambulance siren drops as it drives away from you (the Doppler effect).

The American astronomer Edwin Hubble made a crucial discovery: the further away a galaxy is, the greater its red-shift. This means more distant galaxies are moving away from us faster. This relationship is known as Hubble’s Law and it provided the first observational evidence that the universe is expanding.

If all galaxies are moving away from us, and the most distant ones are moving fastest, the universe must be expanding in every direction. It is not that galaxies are flying through space — space itself is stretching, carrying galaxies with it. Imagine dots drawn on a balloon: as the balloon inflates, every dot moves away from every other dot, and the dots furthest apart move away from each other fastest.

If the universe is expanding now, it must have been smaller in the past. Winding the clock backwards, all the matter and energy in the universe would have been concentrated in an incredibly small, hot, dense point — the starting point for the Big Bang theory.

The Big Bang Theory

The Big Bang theory states that the universe began approximately 13.8 billion years ago from an extremely hot, dense point. Space itself began to expand rapidly, and as it cooled, matter formed — first subatomic particles, then atoms, then stars and galaxies.

Two key pieces of evidence support the Big Bang theory:

  • Red-shift of galaxies — as described above, the observation that all distant galaxies are moving away from us (and the further away, the faster) shows the universe is expanding. Running this expansion backwards points to a single origin.
  • Cosmic microwave background radiation (CMBR) — in 1965, Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson detected faint microwave radiation coming from every direction in space. This is the leftover thermal radiation from the Big Bang itself, now cooled to about −270°C (just 2.7 K above absolute zero). The CMBR is the strongest evidence for the Big Bang because no other theory explains its existence.
Key Fact

The two main pieces of evidence for the Big Bang are red-shift (showing the universe is expanding) and cosmic microwave background radiation (the afterglow of the Big Bang, detected from every direction in space).

Dark Matter and Dark Energy

Scientists have discovered that the visible matter we can see — stars, planets, gas clouds — makes up only about 5% of the total mass-energy of the universe. The rest is made of two mysterious components.

Dark matter accounts for about 27% of the universe. It cannot be seen because it does not emit, absorb or reflect light. Scientists know it exists because galaxies rotate faster than expected from their visible mass — unseen mass must be providing extra gravitational pull.

Dark energy makes up about 68% of the universe. In the late 1990s, scientists studying distant supernovae discovered the expansion of the universe is accelerating. Dark energy is the name given to whatever force is driving this acceleration, but its true nature remains unknown.

Dark matter and dark energy are two of the biggest unsolved problems in physics. Dark matter holds galaxies together but has never been directly detected. Dark energy is pushing the universe apart at an increasing rate, yet its true nature is unknown. Together, they make up about 95% of the universe — we can only directly observe about 5% of everything that exists.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Space physics questions often ask you to describe the life cycle of a star or explain the evidence for the Big Bang. For star life cycle questions, always state the starting point (nebula) and make sure you describe both pathways — Sun-sized stars and massive stars — unless the question specifies one. For Big Bang evidence, name both red-shift and CMBR, and explain what each one shows. A common mistake is describing red-shift without linking it to the expansion of the universe — always make the connection explicit.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Solar system structure — the Sun is a main sequence star orbited by eight planets, with gravity providing the centripetal force for all orbital motion.
  • Star life cycles — all stars begin as nebulae; Sun-sized stars end as white dwarfs, while massive stars explode as supernovae, leaving neutron stars or black holes.
  • Expanding universe — red-shift and cosmic microwave background radiation are the two key pieces of evidence for the Big Bang, and dark energy is causing the expansion to accelerate.

glossary_terms.definition: The Sun and all the objects that orbit it, including eight planets, dwarf planets, moons, asteroids and comets.
A medium-sized star in the stable phase of its life cycle, fusing hydrogen into helium in its core.
The force of attraction between any two objects with mass. It holds planets in orbit around the Sun.
An object that orbits a planet or star. Natural satellites include moons; artificial satellites are human-made objects such as the International Space Station.
An orbit where a satellite takes exactly 24 hours to complete one revolution, so it stays above the same point on Earth's surface.
A large cloud of dust and gas in space from which stars are born when gravity causes the cloud to collapse.
The process by which small atomic nuclei combine to form a larger nucleus, releasing enormous amounts of energy. This powers stars.
A young, contracting star that has not yet begun nuclear fusion in its core.
A large, cool star formed when a main sequence star exhausts its hydrogen fuel and its outer layers expand.
The hot, dense remnant core of a Sun-sized star after it has shed its outer layers. About the size of Earth but extremely dense.
An extremely large, cool star formed when a massive star exhausts its hydrogen fuel. Much bigger than a red giant.
A massive explosion that occurs when a large star collapses at the end of its life, briefly outshining an entire galaxy.
An extremely dense remnant of a massive star after a supernova, composed almost entirely of neutrons. A teaspoon would weigh about a billion tonnes.
A region of space where gravity is so strong that nothing, not even light, can escape from it.
The pattern of dark lines seen when light from a star is split into a spectrum, caused by elements in the star absorbing specific wavelengths.
The shift of light from a galaxy towards longer (redder) wavelengths, indicating the galaxy is moving away from the observer.
The change in frequency or wavelength of a wave as the source moves towards or away from the observer.
The scientific theory that the universe began from an extremely hot, dense point approximately 13.8 billion years ago and has been expanding ever since.
Invisible matter that does not emit or absorb light but exerts a gravitational pull. It is thought to make up about 27% of the universe.
A mysterious force that is causing the expansion of the universe to accelerate. It is thought to make up about 68% of the universe.
